What Is Virtual Try On in Buble?

Virtual try on is an image-to-image app for previewing clothes on a person photo. Upload a clear photo of the person, add a garment product image or a target model outfit reference, then generate a new image that shows how the clothing direction could look on that person. It is built for fast visual decisions, not for replacing size charts, tailoring, or a physical fitting.
Where a Virtual Try On App Is Most Useful

People search for virtual try on when they already have a person photo, a garment image, or a shopping idea and need to see a believable visual preview. These are the jobs the Buble app is designed to support.
How to Use Virtual Try On in Buble

The generator above is the actual virtual try on app. Keep the workflow simple: start with a usable person photo, add a clear clothing reference, choose the garment scope, then inspect the result before using it.
Photo and Garment Inputs That Work Better

Virtual try on quality depends heavily on the source material. The app accepts common image files for both required inputs, and the current configuration allows JPG, PNG, and WebP images up to 10 MB per input.
What Virtual Try On Can and Cannot Promise
A credible virtual try on page should be honest about limits. AI can create a useful visual preview, but it is still an image generation task, not a measurement system or guaranteed fit prediction.

The app uses two required image inputs: your photo and a garment or target-model reference. The reference can be a clothing product image, a flat lay, or another model wearing the outfit.
Control whether the virtual try on should replace the full visible outfit, only the upper body, lower body, a dress or one-piece garment, or a visible layer or accessory.
Use the keep-background option when you want to preserve the original photo context, or choose a clean studio background when the result needs a simpler product-style presentation.
The prompt asks the model to preserve identity, pose, skin tone, camera angle, and non-clothing areas while transferring garment color, texture, silhouette, and layering from the reference.
Works Best as a Styling Draft
Use virtual try on to compare outfit direction, prepare product visuals, plan a wardrobe look, or test an ecommerce creative before committing to a shoot or purchase.
AI try-on output can still misread fabric, occlusion, logos, scale, or body contact. Treat the result as a visual preview and review details before using it in commercial content.
Use a Photo You Have Permission to Edit
Only upload your own photo or a photo you have permission to use. This matters for privacy, consent, and commercial publishing rights.
Prefer Good Lighting and Visible Body Shape
A clear full-body or half-body image with fitted clothing usually works better than a dark, cluttered, far-away, seated, or heavily cropped photo.
Hands, bags, hair, crossed arms, props, and oversized clothing can make it harder to place the new garment cleanly on the body.
Product photos, flat lays, or model photos with visible color, pattern, neckline, sleeves, length, and silhouette give the app better information than tiny or cropped references.
Tell the App What to Preserve
Use the extra direction field for constraints such as keeping shoes unchanged, preserving hairstyle, making a jacket oversized, or focusing only on the upper-body garment.
Use Studio Background for Cleaner Product Looks
If the original room or street scene distracts from the clothing, choose the clean studio background option to make the try-on result easier to review.
It Is Not a Size Recommendation
The generated image can help you judge visual style, but it does not prove the garment size, tailoring, fabric stretch, or real-world comfort. Use merchant size charts and product details for sizing.
Small logos, text, buttons, seams, textures, and patterns may be simplified or changed. Review important brand or product details before publishing.
Hands, hair, bags, jewelry, loose layers, and complex poses are common sources of artifacts because the model must decide which pixels belong in front of the new garment.
Use It as a Decision Aid
The best use of virtual try on is to compare style direction, color, silhouette, and presentation before committing to a purchase, shoot, listing, or campaign asset.

provider.name: REA Chrome DevTools Protocol observation provider

limitations: Observation starts when REA attaches; prior network and console activity is unavailable.

Raw network headers, bodies, cookies, storage values, console objects, and WebSocket payloads are never retained; explicitly requested primitive console text is retained verbatim, while payload captures retain value-free shapes.
Source maps are reported only as declarative URLs and are not fetched.
URL-less scripts and console events without an allowed source URL are excluded because their origin cannot be proven.
Only script bytes retained in this capture are exported. Sources are not refetched or executed, and a response or Debugger source does not prove execution.

Ordinary unambiguous URL paths preserve relative module layouts by origin, including case-distinct spellings. Query variants, exact path collisions, file/directory prefixes, inline sources, and unrepresentable paths are isolated. A case-distinct pair is isolated only when the destination filesystem cannot store both spellings; the record names that pair. Browser module relationships of isolated paths remain unknown.

Local JavaScript analysis does not implement browser import maps, root-relative URL resolution, remote URL loading, or browser runtime behavior. It may strip import queries and fragments; isolated variants are not canonical targets.
Source-map declarations are retained as metadata. No source maps or missing dependencies are fetched or reconstructed.
Captured response bytes are browser-decoded bytes; Debugger sources are the exposed text encoded as UTF-8. Redacted bytes are exported exactly as retained, and may no longer parse as JavaScript.
